title: The temple destroyed
hook: Abdali blew up the Harmandir; tradition says a flying brick struck his nose

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kup Rahira: fighters who lived by speed rode slow, in a ring around their families. Your line was they shielded the families. Who did you slow down for? Today, the Guru's house itself. Day eight hundred sixty-six.

Barrels are carried across the causeway to the Harmandir, the temple in the middle of the pool. Gunpowder. They're packed inside, among the walls where the Granth's hymns had been sung morning and evening. The Sikh families who might have stood there are dead, scattered, or far away, after the killing at Kup Rahira. Ahmad Shah Abdali has come to Amritsar. The fuse is lit. Then the blast, and the stones and bricks fly. Tradition adds one detail that Sikhs still tell. A brick flew from the explosion and struck Abdali on the nose. Today: the temple destroyed.
screen: `GUNPOWDER ON THE CAUSEWAY.` → `THE BLAST.` → `A BRICK STRIKES THE KING.`

segments.voice: Start with the loss, and don't hurry past it. The Harmandir was the Gurus' house, built in the pool Guru Arjan had finished, where the Granth had been installed. And now it was rubble, and tradition says the pool was filled in again. For Sikhs who heard the news, it came on top of the dead at Kup Rahira. The building fell. That's the line, and it's meant to be said plainly. Now the brick. Tradition says the wound on Abdali's nose never properly healed, and some tellings say it troubled him for the rest of his life. That link belongs to the story, not to a record. Sikhs tell it not as a joke and not quite as a miracle, but as a sign that what's done to the Guru's house doesn't simply go away. So what did the Sikhs say was lost, and what wasn't? Here the tradition is very clear. Guru Gobind Singh, before his death, had said the Guru from then on would be the Granth, the scripture, and the Panth, the community of the Khalsa. Sikhs say neither of those could be blown up with a building. That doesn't make the loss small. People had prayed in that room. Their parents had prayed there. But it changes what kind of loss it is. Guru Tegh Bahadur has a line in the Granth, here in paraphrase: whatever has been made will pass away, today or tomorrow. The Sikh scripture doesn't promise that buildings last. It points past them. So today, just sit with what fell. What comes next is tomorrow's story.
screen: `THE GURUS' HOUSE, NOW RUBBLE.` · `A BRICK, AND A WOUND THAT LINGERED.` · `THE GURU: THE GRANTH AND THE PANTH.` · `WHATEVER IS MADE WILL PASS.` · then, large: `THE BUILDING FELL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with loss. Settle, and let the breath go where it wants. Bring to mind a place that's gone, or changed past recognizing. A childhood home, a shop that closed, a room where someone you loved used to sit. Let yourself see it as it was. Don't rush to the bright side, and don't tell yourself it doesn't matter. Just let it be gone, for these two minutes. Then notice, gently, what you still carry from it that no one could knock down. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.

The temple destroyed. Ahmad Shah Abdali had the Harmandir blown up with gunpowder, and tradition says a flying brick struck him on the nose. The building fell; Sikhs say the Guru, in the Granth and the Panth, did not. Today's word.
Your line: the building fell. Today, let one loss be a loss, without rushing to fix it, and notice what's still standing in you. Day eight hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember the destruction of the Harmandir by Ahmad Shah Abdali as part of the eighteenth-century persecutions, and teach that the Guru is the Guru Granth Sahib and the Guru Panth, not any building.

fork.setup: you're a Sikh who has just heard the Harmandir has been blown up, so soon after Kup Rahira. what do you do first?
options: tell yourself it was only a building and move on.
let it be a real loss, and grieve it.
swear you'll never go to Amritsar again.
fork.reveal: the story keeps the loss real: the building fell. what the Sikhs did next is tomorrow's story, at the ruins.

original.note: Gurmukhi: Harimandar, the house of God, the temple at the center of the pool at Amritsar.

trapdoor: what you thought: the temple was destroyed, so the Sikhs lost their Guru.
what it means: the building fell, and the loss was real, but Sikhs say the Guru is the Granth and the Panth.
what a scholar hears: the brick and the lingering wound come from tradition, while Sikh teaching places the Guru in the Granth and the Panth, not in stone.

notes: No date is given (often Vaisakhi 1762); the script places it 'the same year' as Kup Rahira, following the index sequence. Confirm.

The flying brick and the lingering wound (often said to be a cancerous sore on his nose) are given as tradition; the hedge 'not every account makes that link' should be checked by a Keeper or historian.
Paraphrase of Ang 1429 ('jo upjio so binas hai paro aaj kai kaal'): confirm Ang and paraphrase.
'Where the Granth had been installed': confirm.
Guru Gobind Singh's passing of guruship to the Granth and the Panth is stated as Sikh teaching; confirm wording.
Original ਹਰਿਮੰਦਰ and the gloss 'house of God' (Hari, God; mandar, temple): confirm.

Editor pass: cut 'the same year' from the review (a date claim the script can't source); hedged the second filling of the pool as tradition; replaced the 'not every account' manuscript-style claim in the teach and myth; fixed the garbled word-segment line about the Guru, the Granth and the Panth.

Audit pass: 'neither [the Granth nor the Panth] was inside the building' read as a literal claim that no copy of the scripture was there, which the script can't source; now 'Sikhs say neither could be blown up with a building' (teach and myth).
